Catalog Kids Methodology

Methodology

What the number means.

Acuity asks one question of every title: how much does watching this enrich the mind behind your eyes? That cognitive read is the spine of the score — and we temper it with how the title actually landed, both with the audiences who watched it and the critics who reviewed it. Here is exactly how we turn all of that into a single number.

One scale, three dimensions

The cognitive core of the score begins with three independent dimensions, each graded from 0 to 100:

Depth

How much the title asks of you — structural complexity, ambiguity, layered plotting, and ideas that reward a second pass. High scores demand attention.

Insight

What you carry out of it — history, science, character of a real place or person, a discipline made legible. How much you simply know that you didn't before.

Craft

Whether the thing is actually made well — writing, performance, direction, and the cohesion that separates a considered work from a competent one.

Three inputs, one number

Those dimensions don't stand alone. The Acuity Quotient is a blend of three signals, so the number reflects not just what we think a title demands of you, but how it actually landed:

  • Cognitive value — the Depth, Insight, and Craft scores above, combined into a single composite. This is our own read of what a title gives the mind.
  • Audience reception — how the broad base of IMDb users rate the title. Every title in the catalog carries this signal.
  • Critic reception — the professional verdict, read from Metacritic and Rotten Tomatoes. It is the sharpest counterweight to a popular but slight title, and the strongest endorsement of a difficult but accomplished one.

Critic coverage is strongest for popular, widely-reviewed titles; the deeper into the long tail you go, the more a title leans on its cognitive read and its audience score alone. Where no critic has weighed in yet, the other two inputs carry the number — and the title's detail page says so plainly rather than inventing a verdict.

Those three inputs are blended into a single composite, then placed on a wide, IQ-style scale we call the Acuity Quotient — a deliberate nod to a familiar standardized measure. The median title sits at 100 and the scale runs up to roughly 200. The number is a measure of a title's overall value, not a ranking position — and because the scale is anchored to the whole catalog, it recalibrates as the catalog grows: add thousands more titles and every score is re-derived from the same method, so a 130 means the same thing tomorrow as it does today.

A deliberately flattened curve

Most rating sites drift upward until almost everything is "great" and the scale stops meaning anything. We do the opposite — but we also refuse the other trap, the tall central spike that buries every title in the middle. The Acuity Quotient is calibrated into a single, bell-shaped hump centered on a median of 100, with a standard deviation of about 37. It is intentionally flatter than a normal distribution: we push real weight outward toward the ends, so the top and bottom of the scale are populated rather than empty. Most titles still cluster near the middle, but genuine brilliance and genuine noise both have room to live in tails that actually carry titles.

This is the credibility test for the whole project, so we show our work. Here is the distribution of every Acuity Quotient in the catalog:

Each bar is the number of titles at a given Acuity Quotient, colored by the tier that score falls into. A near-zero skew keeps the hump symmetric, while the flattened shape and weighted tails keep the ends of the scale from emptying out. Click a tier in the key to isolate its band.

The five tiers

Numbers are precise but cold, so each title also falls into one of five named bands, drawn by fixed cut-points on the scale and color-coded consistently everywhere on the site. The names describe how much a title asks of you — from Idle background to something genuinely Profound.

Where the facts come from

The factual scaffolding — titles, years, genres, audience ratings, and vote counts — is drawn from public IMDb datasets, and the critic scores (Metacritic and Rotten Tomatoes) come through OMDb. Streaming availability reflects US services and is illustrative; when a title has no availability on record, we say so rather than guess. The scores themselves are ours: computed by a single, repeatable method from those public signals, never hand-tuned title by title.

Because one canonical dataset drives every page, a title's number is identical wherever you meet it — the catalog, its detail page, a head-to-head comparison. Update the data, and the whole site updates with it. There is no second, editorial set of numbers hiding behind the first.

What it is not

A high Acuity Quotient is not a command and a low one is not an insult. Comfort viewing earns a low cognitive load by design, and that is a perfectly good reason to watch something. Acuity is a measuring instrument, not a verdict on your taste — its only job is to tell you, plainly, what a given hour is likely to give back.

Sources & credits

The factual layer beneath every score comes from public datasets, and we credit it plainly. Title metadata — names, release years, genres, audience ratings, and vote counts — is drawn from IMDb's public datasets and is used here for non-commercial purposes only. Reception scores — audience ratings alongside the Metacritic and Rotten Tomatoes critic verdicts — are retrieved via OMDb. Poster artwork is served directly from TMDB's image servers and is never downloaded or rehosted: we simply hotlink each image so the credit and the bytes both stay with their source.

This product uses the TMDB API but is not endorsed or certified by TMDB. The Acuity Quotient, its three dimensions, and the tiers are our own computed work, layered on top of these public facts — the numbers are ours, the underlying data is theirs.
